blocks.x: I'll make a note here, this is continuing the Kid Thomas interview, this is December the 10th over at 600 Charters again, and we'll continue talking about this photograph that you loaned us very kindly, this picture, quite an old picture of your band, can you tell us just who's at all there? That's Albert. The trombone. Yeah. Albert, what's the name again?
It's Tom Albert's boy.
Oh, Tom Albert's boy, oh sure, yeah that's right, his son.
No.
I thought the, and the banjo.
Elton Theodore. Elton Theodore.
Theodore.
Ruchon. Ruchon is the bass. Yeah. And this is, Tom Anderson.
That's the drummer.
Yeah.
And the clarinetist is Steve. Steve Andrum.
The bass.
Yeah. And of course Kid Thomas on the. Yeah, and me. Got your music rack up on there too. Looks about like this one I had.
Then that's another band.
Oh, this is the band on the ferry boat, this little tiny. Yeah, yeah. We probably won't be able to take a picture that's too small to duplicate.
Yeah, yeah.
About when was, oh when was this big picture taken about? Woo.
I mean I had been around about, around about, around until the time of depression.
Back in the 1930s then?
Yeah, around that time. Mm-hmm.
Just when did you move down here from Reserve? Around, let's see, after the first war.
It was around about nine.

The war was over I think in 1918, wasn't it? November. Yeah, I was going 22. Around 1922 you moved here. Mm-hmm. Oh, you were telling about your card, your business card, mentioning your band that you gave out to the Tip Top. And I forgot to tell you then, I had a real old card, maybe a couple of old cards that date way back. And if I remember, I may be wrong, you let me know. It says Kid Thomas and his Bolo Sweets band. Is that right? No, no, no, no, it wasn't no Bolo Sweets. Well then it's somebody else's band. You didn't have that, huh?
No, no, no, not Bolo. It was always Kid Thomas band, jazz band.
Yeah, I'm going to look up that card after a while and see if I can find it.
It was jazz, you see? Yeah. Uh-huh. See, like now we got it not Dixieland, you see, but it was jazz, you know what I mean? That was when we first had them made, you know what I mean?
The jazz band.
Uh-huh. So, well, now.
Where did you live when you first moved down here?
I live, uh, wait.
On this side of the river, was it?
This side of the river. I live up on.
Uptown?
No, Clio Street. Oh yeah. I was on Clio Street when I first came here. Then I moved from Clio, then I moved on, uh, I went over the river and lived over the river.
Yeah, now this picture again, to get back to that, was that taken when you were living across the river or over here?
That's when I lived across the river. Over across the river. Yeah, I took that, I took that on St. Charles Street. Yeah.
I noticed you have the band, you have the band caps on.
Uh-huh.
Did you use those same caps on the street when you'd march? Same cap, uh-huh.
Everything, see them jackets, see shirts is blue. Oh the shirts are blue. It's a real light blue because it looks white here.
Yeah, that's right, yeah. What about the pants look almost white here?
Yeah, white pants too.
White pants. White pants.
And the blue, uh, jacket.
And the caps. And the caps. Yeah.
And cap, white top, you see.
White top on the cap. Yeah, white top.
And we took that in a small, uh, it was a small studio, see. A little photo studio.
Uh-huh. Oh, then this other, this picture of you down below.
I took that in Morel from, uh, one of them, uh, flying horses, you know, tent. Oh yes. Yeah, flying horse tent. How about I took that? Me and Joe took one like that, you see. Yeah. Uh-huh.
Oh, and the other little tiny picture there.
You took that on the Cunhares Street ferry boat.
Who all was in the band? I can't hardly see anybody there.
Well, you see I had a boy called Alvin. He was playing drums. Alvin Clemons, he did, you know him. Alvin Clemons, what he called, Bokeye, Wilford Bokeye.
Is he a sax player or what? Yeah, saxophone player.
Uh-huh.
He's the fellow that was over there once when I heard him a couple years ago. Yeah, Bokeye.
Bokeye. And, uh, and you got, how many you got there?
One, two, three, four, five. Six, eh? I want to see five for sure. Five there.
Yeah.
Somebody else.
No, that, that, that, that was Bokeye. That, that was, uh, John Smith. Oh.
Yeah. Who is the bass player on one end holding his bass?
That's the, Bouchon. The same fellow, don't you? Yeah, yeah, same fellow, huh?
Up above.
Uh-huh.
Same fellow.
Yeah.

Uh-huh. I remember you told us once that trip when you had a job over here and then you had to get across the river and almost ran off into the river. When you came down that ramp. Yeah, that's right. That's true. I did. I think we have that on the life tape.

Uh-huh, yeah. That's when, I tell you, when we played down on the feet. We played down on the feet then. Yeah. Uh-huh. Because we had to cross a little, pull a barge, you know? You had to pull that barge with a stick, you know what I mean? Yes. And we used to play down that, down that, by a tarot road, you see? And so the man, you see, the question about it was Bill, when we knock off, the tarot we knock off, you know, it'd be late. Well the man would be at home sleeping. Then you go wake the man up, you know how each man would get up all excited. Yeah. And he forgot to tie the boat. Oh. Yeah, he forgot to tie the flat that it was a barge like, you see? And so I guess the man told him, and the thing, if the car's coming off, the thing was pulling away from the bank, you know? Yeah. Then we hollered at the man, you know what I mean? Coming off and went in that barge, you know? Yeah. So this boy had it, it's Sero, Elton Sero had a fold, you see? And a multi-fold, that's what he had, you know what I mean? So, well after that, well, the thing was all right then, the man tied the thing up, you know what I mean? He tied it up. And later on, and then they built a bridge, you know what I mean, on them turntables, you see? They built that. So from that, well, we used to play down there every Saturday night. Yeah. We used to play every Saturday night down there for a lady called Miss Lillian. She's dead now, and she had a pavilion there on the bayou. We used to play for her every Saturday night. Then we turned around, after she died, her sister had a place too. Played for her on Saturday night. So, and then white boy, white fella used to take us down sometime in a little truck. White fella, you know? Yeah. He used to take us down in a little truck and sometimes we'd play there sometimes at three and four o'clock in the morning, you know what I mean? Late hours at night, but we used to make a lot of money, you know what I mean? Tips, you know? Yeah. And things fell, you'd go around with the hat, you know, pick up so much. Oh yeah. You know how much you'd pick up? Because pick up a hundred dollars, make no difference playing no more than that one hour, you know what I mean? So, well that fella, that man there, he was living in Gretna. You know what I mean? He used to hustle for us, you know? Like you said, we played him overtime, you see? He hustled. And he had a fella up here in Gretna, up in Moreira. He used to have a store. I don't know if he still has this store. But this fella was a man, you know what he do? He come around, see like he beat at the dances. See like one fella said, he put up ten dollars. That's the pay of overtime, you see? You know what he do? That fella put up ten dollars, he put twenty. See?
Yeah, pretty good.

But he had money, this fella you see. So well from one dollar to dollar like that, you know what I mean? He took up so much money. He don't want one dollar, you see? That's all. Don't care how much he would pick up, you know what I'm talking about. So well later on this fella, later on after that fella come back for me to play, when we play down on the island, down in the Gulf of Mexico.
See?

That's they call the Grand Isles, you know? Yeah. Well that same man, what I'm telling you about, he bought a boat. He bought a boat from the Gulf of Mexico. One of them submarine chasers, you know? Oh, that was a fast thing. And he used to charge two dollars a head, see? Well, two dollars a head had two decks. One bottom and the upper deck, you know what I mean? Well he used to do all the gambling down there, you see? So well he used to charge two dollars a head for people to go down. Well most people used to go down and most everybody, they think people was kind of well off people, you had money, you know? Yeah. Like big time fellas who fish go fishing and different things like that. See, well the poor people, well they couldn't afford it, you know what I mean? So we'd go down on that boat, every Saturday we'd go down on that boat, see? But that one fella, he had a little yacht, it was a good sized yacht. Well he used to take us down too on his yacht. Well that's the very man who'd come got us to play for these people. Oh yeah? Yeah, because you see he know Joe, he know Joe because he lived up in Warrick, well this man he did. And he used to come by my house and got me, see me, I'll never forget he was in a fold, a mile of their fold. Came there one morning and we was the first club band to play down there, because you couldn't go down there unless you'd go on a boat. On a boat. They had no, now you see now they have a road now, you see? You go all the way to wrestling, then you cross the bridge, then you go to Lockport, go all the way down now, you see, gold medal. Well then we played on every Saturday, we played Saturday, Sunday, matinee and that night. Then we'd come back that Sunday morning, Monday morning at least, you see, we'd come back. And well I tell you, now the first man we played for, the first man we played for, it was the man when that man first come to get us to work, well Mr. Adam. Well he had a pavilion, he had two dance pavilion, you see. So after-
It was old Grand Iowa?

Grand Iowa, old Grand Iowa. Faced right on the Gulf, you know what I mean? Yeah. Well we played for him, and we played quite a while for him, and then after that we left from there we'd start playing for this other fellow. So we played every Saturday and Sunday. So until after, well, things began to get boom, after they started to build the road. See after they built the road, well people, a lot of different traffic going there you see. So the man just quit giving dances. He quit, you see, he quit giving the dances. But afterwards, well this fellow, he drive cab, got cab at Canal Street Fair there now. He's got a nightclub down there, see that was built lately, that was afterwards, you know what I mean? They didn't have all that down there, and they had no more to dance hall. That's all they had. So well he built a club down there, and so well I never did play for him, but he wanted, he had asked me to work for him, but we were working at the time, you know? So I never had a chance to play for him. So another fellow they called Tony, he had to play style there, you see, or he had to be able to afterwards, you see. He tried to get us to come down and play where we was working there, you see. So then we used to play all in, we used to play cut off, we played lockport, cut off, wrestling, gold medal, all the way down, to the end, you see. Thibodeau, Homer, all them places, you know what I mean? Back of Thibodeau, front of Thibodeau, all over, for people you see. Then we played a dance one time on an island. These people live on an island with nothing but water.
Real island?
Real island, Mr. Bill, there's nothing but water. You know, all the, you know what I mean, they got them, what you call it, you know, built on them piling, you see.
Oh, like the big shrimp drying platform? Yeah, yeah, sure, yeah, drying platform, you see.

Well this guy, I tell you, this fellow, this fellow, must have been some Chinaman, you know. Man, just as far as you could look, Mr. Bill, you could see nothing but swamps. Man, swamps, that big as a lobster almost.
Six inches long. Yeah, big as a lobster almost.

You know what I mean? Because I asked the fellow, I said, I said, why y'all get all these big large swamps? He said, well, you know, you see, when we catch the swamps, you know, we sort them out. Yeah. They sort them out, you see. And they takes them and they boil, put them in a big boiler, and boil it, you see. And then they dry it. You see, that's how you can get dry swamps in the grocery store, you know. Yeah, yeah. And then they dry it all, then if they don't do that, they take the swamps and they spread them all on a platform. Just as far as you could look, Mr. Bill, you could see nothing but swamps on that platform.
Right on the wood they put them?

Yeah, right on the platform. Don't put any paper or anything? No, no, no, no, just right on the platform. A platform made like this, like this snow, you see. And just as far as you could look. And then the fellow, the fellow used to have one of them rollers, you know them rollers, like the road on the street when they put the asphalt. All right, they used to have one of them, one like that, and one man sat on it and the other one pulled it. See, that's the crack. You see, that's the crack the hull, you see. Yeah. You see, when the hull, when the swim dries, when it cracks the hull, when they put it in the middle, it won't have less, they'll have to peel off. Yeah. And that swim dust, that swim dust, and they take all that swim dust and they put it away for fertilizer, you see. So.
Well they don't eat all that shrimp then.
No, no, no, they sell that. I mean, do they eat any of that?
Yeah, they eat. They eat, but the shell they sell.
They sell the shell, shrimp dust, you see.
Do they walk right on top of those shrimp when they roll them? Oh yeah, they walk all over that. They walk all over them. Sure, sure they walk all over the shrimp.

The man got that roller, you know, going on it, running on it, you see. And then the man goes and he takes a paddle, you see, he got a big long paddle made like a shovel, he turns them over, you see, so they can dry, you know, just as far as you could look, you don't see nothing much swim. That's all you see. So I asked the man, I said, he said, no, you all don't get that kind of swim. I said, because we saw all the swimps, the lois, this one out, you see. You know what I mean, for the pudding cans and different things like that, you know, dry. So well we played that for them fellas on that island. We played till four o'clock in the morning. Four o'clock in the morning we left and come back that morning on the boat. See, on the boat. So well then that was for a fella, you know, where they get a big dance party for all the swimmers, you know what I mean, fellas fish and this and this and this, you know. There was a big party for all the people who worked on the boat and trawl swimmers. So well from after that, well, things began to get a little slack after a lot of traffic began to, you know what I mean, visit down there, you know. So we started playing and we come back and we played, playing racely. Then we played racely and then so after we left from Neverland we came back and started playing that over here, up here on Lopold in Chapitula. We used to play there, we used to play Friday, yeah, Wednesday Friday and Sunday.
What was that place called, do you remember?
I forgot what the name of that thing, I forgot what the name of that place. It's right on the corner of Lopold in, what's it called, the street, Charter. Not Charter or.
Napoleon and Chapitula.
Chapitula, what I mean.
I remember Albert Burbank played up there once, I can't remember what it was called, something like Harmony Inn but that isn't right.
I can't remember what it was called.
Was it ever called the Tin Roof? No, no, that was the Tin Roof there.
That was the Tin Roof. Do you remember the Tin Roof?
I remember the Tin Roof, no, that was the Tin Roof. Where was that?
That was just further up, just right around in that block in there, but a couple blocks from that.
On Chapitula's?
Yeah, on Chapitula's. Not on Napoleon. Not on Napoleon, uh-huh. No, you see. So I never didn't, I don't remember that name there. I don't remember that name, Mr. Bell.
I remember someplace, I'll look it up in my notes.

But this boy, his boy was an Italian boy, his name was Sam you know. So well we used to play there on Wednesday, Friday, and we couldn't play Saturday because we was playing in wrestling you see, every Saturday. Then after that the war, then the war, second war, broke out. So that made us, we was playing on Chapitula, we was playing for this fella so that's why this fella, Speck, he wanted us to wait for him. He's building a new dance hall. Moulin Rouge. Moulin Rouge, you see. In fact, Speck already had a dance hall, they're on Walkerstown Road, you know what I mean. Them fellas double crossed him, you see. They sold the place, the man sold the place under his nose without telling him. Oh yeah. You see, but he had been, he was there, Speck was there, on that corner when they didn't have nothing but a house and a little grocery store. And we used to play in there, three pieces, me, Joey and that boy, Buckeye. Three piece bootlegging, he used to bootleg lick the leg, you see. And there was nothing. So after that, well, he used to give dances for colored, maybe he might give dances for colored one month or so many weeks for colored then he reversed it to white. See, so many weeks for white. While he was doing that, he wanted to see which race he could make the more his business off. You know what I mean? Yeah. If it's colored or white, it wasn't ever there, well he was going to turn it in. If it had been colored, he could do more things with color, he was going to turn it for colored. So well after he found that corner was better for white, so he turned it all in together for white. So well after that, what he did, he asked the man to build a dance hall, you see. So after that man, the man said well he didn't have no money, so well this other fellow, the fellow crossed the bar, you see. He crossed, facing him over the bar. Well he has a milk barrier. You see, well he told Speck, he said well if this fellow don't have the money to build a play for you, I'll build a dance off here on that side of the highway. You know what I mean? So finally well him and Speck, this fellow got together and Speck, he got the money, you know, he borrowed the money and the man, you know, so much money and the man supposed to pay him back. So well, finally well, after he got the place all fixed up and everything, we still playing for him, you see, but after we, we only was using three pieces at a time in that house, but after that we started using six, you see, seven pieces at least. So we played there a while for him in the new place, we opened a new place for him, you see, then we left there and went back to wrestling again, you see. So after we went back to wrestling. So there, well, we went back to wrestling with playing La Ponte Chapitula, you see. So that's how he come to build this dance hall, he had nothing out there, Moulin Rouge, during the time of the war he built that. See when lumber, you couldn't get lumber like you want, you know what I mean? You see, lumber was scarce, everything was scarce, you know what I mean? You couldn't get lumber. So he's going all over different parts of the country, you know what I mean, buying buildings, you know, to build that place. So he told Joe, he said, yeah, he told Joe, he said, Joe, I'd like to get y'all to play work for me in my new dance hall. So Joe asked him, what's the matter? He said, man, he sold the place, man went sold the place, a fella called Thomas C. Had the Midway Park. Oh really? Yeah, he had the Midway Park, you see. He said, they double crossed me. So he said, I ain't, I'm, the show ain't gonna, the show ain't gonna make me, you know what I ain't gonna hang on, let him outdo me, you see. So, after he completed that place, he hired us to play. So he said, well, he told Joe, he said, well, I'd like to get a good size band, you know. Well, I had a good size band, so sometime, sometime I'll have 14 piece bands, you know, sometime 14 piece bands, you know what I mean? So, he, well we played there all during that war. Until, you know, after the war we had to take, begin to drop off. We left from there and we went back to Raceland again. Oh hell. Yeah, we go back to Raceland again. We go back there and start playing. So finally, all right, went back to Raceland, so finally he, he still operated and gave a dance, but he went and got hired a cowboy band, because you know what I mean, Ben's that drop off, you see. You know what I mean? You want a smaller band, you know what I mean? You want to cut out on our band, you see. Well, we was going to, well, we was going to cast, we always did cast seven pieces, no less than seven, you know what I mean? So, well, so, well, so, we're going to cut out on the band, so that's how we left him. So, well, finally, he came back again for us. Start playing for him again. Come back, playing for him again. So, after we come back, play for him again, we played a long time for him again, then we left for him again. So, place went down, he rented, he rented the place out. He rented the place out to the two brother-laws from Mississippi, two brother-laws. So one of the brothers now had the keyhole in West Vigo, and the other one had the Moulin Rouge. So, right, so the man doing pretty good minutes. Now he wants to play his back. But you know when you lease up, you can't get it back just like that, you know, you got to wait until he leaves up, man. But all right, so the man was doing pretty good. So we started playing for that man, you see. So this man, he's hillbilly, you see, he comes from Mississippi, he's breathing hillbilly music. So while we played, we played quite a while for him too, well he won't get a hillbilly band, you know what I mean? So all right. He got the hillbilly band, so we left for him again. We played somewhere else, somewhere else, somewhere else, you know what I mean? So anyhow, so after he got the place back, he come back and got us again. Yeah. And then we played for him, played for him a long time. Then way after a while he let go again. Then the last time we played, that's when he turned into gambling. That's the last time, you see. So that's why he made his mistake when he done that, you know what I mean?
That's when the new sheriff came in there.

Yeah, that's right. Yeah, you see. So he turned into gambling, gambling didn't last all that long, you know what I mean? So that's why after the thing he gave me, he couldn't do nothing with it, so he rented out that his boy got it now, you see. So well, anyhow.
I remember ten years ago you used to play other places along there too.
Yeah.
Down Moore and Harvey, wasn't it? What were some of the other places you played?
Harvey?
Wasn't it down the road a little bit farther, away from the river, on the other side of the road, you played someplace?

Well I played, Mr. Bill, look I played, I played at Al J's Country Club way down low cove way in the back. Oh yeah. I played, I used to play for a fella by the river here, right by the river. I used to play for a fella, he had a dance hall. I played for him, Mr. Watney, he had a dance hall. I played for him and so many people I played for.
You played about all of them over there. Oh yeah, but a lot. There were a lot of dance halls on that side of the river, there still are. There were plenty of dance halls, see.
Oh I remember one night, I forgot I was going to ask you.

You were telling about, you know when it was a little bit slow getting started there this winter, how one time that they, you said you could get the crowd coming there, what was that you used there? Oh yeah, you were talking about the bus?
Flaxseed or something?
Flaxseed or something?

Flaxseed, what was it? Flaxseed? Flaxseed, yeah you see, I tell her, we was playing in the country, you see. We used to go to play in the country, or we used to go, you see like holidays coming there now? Yeah. We would miss playing all them holidays in the country, you see. So the boy we was playing for, this boy Sero, you know he came from that St. James Parish, you know. Oh yeah. Well this boy, him and this boy grew up together, see. Well every time we'd have a dance ball we'd high in the play. So we'd go, we'd go out there. Well most of the time we'd go, make no difference, it wouldn't be no, it could be any other night, Saturday night or Sunday night, it wouldn't make no difference. Most of the time we'd go to always have a dance elsewhere, you know maybe. The dance wouldn't be that close, it'd be a couple of miles apart, you see. So this man he'd be worried you know. You see well, and the band they used to have, in them days, a lot of pretty good bands, you see, there was good bands, you see. Man sometimes Cleven Williams would be playing them dances there, different bands, good bands, you know what I mean. So I used to tell him all the time, we used to tell him all the time, man, say we ain't worried about them bands, because we going to close them up. Just like that. He said, how you know? I said, man we going to close them people up. So to make him, you know what I mean, to make him convinced, I said, you know what you do? I said, you go to the drugstore and get your butter, maybe a couple of pounds of flaxseed, just sprinkle it all up and down from the dance hall, from them people's dance hall to your
dance hall.
I said, that's how boys feed. You see Mr. Bill, you take for instance, look, you take a boy at a chicken, man you could put something, corn.
Yeah they'll follow that down there, you know.

Tilt it in. Well that's how people do. You see, well so, well he did that. And sure man for nine o'clock that place was closed up. Closed up. Sure, and we used to close them all down, Mr. Bill. That didn't matter. We used to, every time we go, I don't care what band we be playing out there, we close them people down flat. Clabon Williams, band from here.
I'm telling. I remember you told once, you sent some, was it some musician out to get some flaxseed? Yeah, John Smith. And they got the, you know.

He was playing right on Bourbon Street at the old Haymarket. Right there, I'm going to tell you where that was Mr. Bill, and right there going, a couple blocks going toward Conair Street. Yeah. On the corner there. Right on the corner. You know right on the corner there, you see right on the corner they got a place there where they don't show nothing but, but have shows there I believe. Yeah. On this side the bank it.
Yeah, maybe it's El Morocco or something. Yeah, round in there.

Round Long in there, but it's about a couple blocks from Conair Street. Yeah. You know. So the Haymarket was up in there somewhere, up in there, in that block there, you know. So this old man, you know, he had a nightclub and he couldn't get nobody in that club. Nobody wouldn't come there. And with Chico was playing, he had a nightclub across the street.
Yeah.
What's this guy name in his wife's house? Got this man in here now.
Sid DeVilla for a while had one there.
Oh, no. Prima.
Yeah. Leon Prima.
Yeah, he crossed the street here. Yeah. You see? All right. So we was playing there, you know.
So couldn't get nobody in that play.

So we was talking, me and John, you know. I said, John, we going to get somebody in this place here tonight. So I said, man you go, I said go to the drugs, so he went on Conair and Rapporty. He went and got some, I told him to get the whole grain, you know. He went and got the powder. And man, when he came back he had powder all over his clothes, all over his face.
I asked him, I said, what are you care for man?
I said, look at you being a flower bear, you know. So he had it all over his clothes. I said, oh, I said, that was you done wrong. Because good clothes. All on his clothes that way.
But he said, I'll spray.

And you know what I'm saying Mr. Bill? I wouldn't tell you what, you know we had some people in that place. But they did pack it, huh? Yeah, well it's funny how that'll work sometimes. And look, and from that day we never told that man how that people come to the company. And well all right, that very night we did that, and that very night we left. See we left, it was going to be on the Christmas, you see. They was going to play somewhere else, going somewhere else and play, you see. And the boy that got tied playing. We played a long time on Bourbon Street there. So, and from that time we never told the old man nothing. You know what I mean? So this old man, you know, since he couldn't get nobody in his club, he used to have a fellow used to come there. Every night that fellow would come, musical tax, you know. He used to come collect. Well the old man, the old man owed about $500 musical tax. But every time he come, he never gets to catch the old man. The old man duck him, you know. So, so that's the only time that old man made money that night. That one, that one special night. But all them other nights we played there, couldn't get nobody up in that place.
